Summary  
Data source overview: The provided text is a short mathematical proof and theorem establishing necessary and sufficient matrix-inequality conditions (H ⪰ MᱼMᱼᵀ) for a Hessian H to make a function strongly convex with respect to arbitrary norms, with concrete simplifications for the ℓ², ℓ¹ and ℓ∞ cases. Although no AI-safety interventions are stated explicitly, strong convexity of training objectives is closely tied to optimisation stability and therefore to reliability of trained AI systems.  

EXTRACTION CONFIDENCE[73]  
The extraction converts the purely theoretical content into an AI-safety relevant knowledge fabric by (i) identifying the downstream risk of optimisation instability, (ii) tracing the causal reasoning through the proof to actionable design interventions that enforce strong convexity, and (iii) explicitly marking all steps that relied on light or moderate inference with lower edge confidences. The JSON was validated for naming consistency and edge connectivity.

Inference strategy justification: Because the paper contains only abstract mathematics, moderate inference (edge-confidence 1–2) was required to map the results to practical AI-safety interventions such as Hessian-based regularisation and standard ℓ² regularisation. These are the most direct, widely accepted ways practitioners operationalise strong convexity guarantees.

Extraction completeness explanation: All distinct reasoning steps in the proof that are necessary for the causal chain from “instability risk” to “regularise the Hessian” are represented as nodes. Two parallel implementation mechanisms (general MᱼMᱼᵀ constraint and simpler ℓ² identity constraint) are included to capture the branching offered by the theorem. No isolated nodes remain.

Key limitations  
1. The source offers no empirical validation; the “Mathematical proof” node is used as validation evidence, which may overstate practical effectiveness.  
2. Real-world training often involves non-convex objectives; mapping convexity results to deep learning required inference.  
3. Section headings were absent; “Proof.” and “Theorem.” were used as the closest references.
